narrative.text: The table of contents of the data quality self-assessment tool, followed by acknowledgements of the countries and offices that tested it and GAVI's financial support.
A near-empty acknowledgements section containing only page numbers.
The list of abbreviations used in the immunization data quality self-assessment tool, from AD syringe and AEFI to VVM.

The executive summary describes the DQS as a flexible toolbox for assessing immunization monitoring systems at district and health unit levels, aimed at national and regional staff who adapt it. It aims to check the accuracy of reported immunization numbers and the quality of monitoring practices, in support of the Reaching Every District approach. Findings are analysed to identify strengths, weaknesses and practical recommendations, with the goal of building the most relevant options into routine practice.
A footnote describing the Reaching Every District strategy and its five parts, from reaching the underserved to involving local communities in planning sessions.

Presents the DQS toolbox options, summarised in a table of what can be assessed at district and health unit level. It explains in detail how to check reporting and recording accuracy by recounting immunizations across tally sheets, registers and reports and calculating accuracy ratios. Further sections cover completeness and timeliness of reporting, quality questions on the monitoring system, immunization card recording, vaccine wastage and safety monitoring. It ends with coverage denominators, which are explored through adaptable questions on quality.

Advises visiting at least three and at most six health units per district, since precision gains level off beyond six, and stresses that discussion of findings matters more than exact figures. It discusses how to select districts and health units and notes that results from one district cannot be extrapolated, though common problems can be shared through feedback.

Explains how to present DQS findings, using accuracy ratios in tables and bar charts with worked examples, and how to compare districts or the same district over time. It also covers presenting completeness, timeliness, quality index scores and wastage results, and mentions supporting spreadsheet workbooks.

Recommends introducing the DQS through a national workshop followed straight away by field assessments, and lists the workshop aims. In the first phase participants review monitoring tools and design and test their own assessment, and in the second they carry out fieldwork before reconvening to analyse results and make recommendations. It also advises involving local partners and academic institutions to sustain the work.

Describes what a successful assessment should produce, such as a documented monitoring system, identified strengths and weaknesses, recommendations used to adjust microplans and supervision, and a follow-up plan. It discusses ways to build the self-designed tool into routine practice, and the block ends with part of an example monitoring chart of DTP doses and drop-out rates.
Annex B gives an example table for tracking the completeness and timeliness of health unit reports received at the district office, with definitions of cumulative completeness and timeliness.

Annex C lists standard questions to assess the quality of the immunization monitoring system at district and health unit levels, with comments and weights. They cover recording, archiving, reporting, demographic data and use of data, such as vaccine ledgers, adverse event procedures and dated reports. The block ends with the start of a child immunization card exercise listing children due for vaccines.
Annex D completes a child immunization card exercise for 20 infants, listing each child's history and due vaccines, with the correct totals for BCG, DTP and measles doses.

Annex E describes how to randomly select health units with probability proportional to size using systematic sampling, with a worked district example based on cumulative DTP3 numbers. It explains choosing a sampling interval and random start, and ends with a random number table.

Annex F sets out a nine-day schedule for a data quality self-assessment workshop, covering monitoring tools, designing quality questions, supervision, sampling, data accuracy, fieldwork, analysis and presentation of results.
The front matter of WHO's 2005 immunization data quality self-assessment (DQS) tool, with a partly garbled title, document code, ordering details, copyright and disclaimer.
